Shares of Booking Holdings (BKNG) have lost 17.2% over the past year, lagging the S&P 500 and its 17.4% return. Following that decline, the stock trades at 17.3 times earnings. That multiple sits below the company's average of 28.3 over its last 12 fiscal quarter ends. A lower P/E means paying less for each dollar of profit, but that discount only pays off if the profit keeps growing. So what would have to go right for Booking Holdings stock to climb from here?

Booking Holdings Would Gain Most From Selling More Travel

Selling more travel would generate most of the stock's potential gain. Under Trefis's three-year scenario, higher revenue accounts for 82.4% of the upside. That means more room nights, the nights travelers book through platforms like Booking.com, alongside more flight and attraction tickets. Following these assumptions, the stock would appreciate about 49% in three years, excluding dividends.

An expanding multiple provides a further 28.4% of the upside, assuming a higher P/E, while a lower margin takes 10.8% back. This scenario lifts the P/E from 17.3 to 19.4. Even after that increase, the multiple would remain below the stock's own 12-quarter average of 28.3.

Where Booking Holdings' Sales Growth Comes From

The scenario models revenue growth of 11.6% a year. That pace falls slightly behind the 12.9% Booking Holdings delivered over the twelve months to fiscal Q2 2026. Growth slowed in the latest quarter, so the scenario needs the pace to pick up again as travelers book more nights and more of the rest of their trips through the company's sites. Room nights increased 5% and revenue rose 8% in fiscal Q2 2026, management said on the August 4, 2026 call. Executives issued a slower guide for the following period, forecasting fiscal Q3 2026 revenue growth of 4% to 6%. However, that guidance covers a single quarter rather than three years, and it assumes the conflict in the Middle East keeps weighing on long-haul travel.

Booking Holdings is also capturing more business from its most loyal customers. Members of its Genius levels 2 and 3 accounted for more than 30% of active customers in fiscal Q2 2026, representing an increase from a year earlier. Management also said that trips combining several bookings grew more than twice as fast as total transactions at Booking.com.

title: Up 10% in the Last Two Weeks, Is Airbnb the Perfect Stock for Today's Market?

Up 10% in the Last Two Weeks, Is Airbnb the Perfect Stock for Today's Market?

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) has mostly been a disappointment for investors after initially surging out of the gate in its 2020 IPO, but in 2026, the stock is finally gaining momentum.

The #1 home-sharing platform has delivered better-than-expected growth, solid margins, and it's leveraging AI to improve user satisfaction. Meanwhile, it is expanding its platform with expanded experiences and guest services offerings.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Over the last two weeks, the stock is up 9.4%, even as the S&P 500 has fallen 1.6%, as the chart below shows.

ABNB data by YCharts

Airbnb's gains have come as the tech sector has tumbled on concerns about an AI bubble and rising interest rates. However, the company has demonstrated its resilience and is well-positioned to thrive in such an environment. Here are three reasons why Airbnb is poised to be a winner in today's stock market.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. It wins on high interest rates

Stock investors generally dislike rising interest rates. After all, higher interest rates tend to make the bond market more attractive, leading investors to rotate out of stocks and into bonds. Additionally, higher interest rates put pressure on high-priced stocks like much of the tech sector, as it makes future earnings less valuable due to a higher discount rate in the discounted cash flow.

Normally, a company like Airbnb would be susceptible to that pressure, but the home-sharing leader actually earns significant profit from interest income thanks to the funds it holds in between customer bookings and disbursement. Through the first half of the year, it's earned $363 million in interest income, more than a third of its before-tax profit, and that number is likely to go up as interest rates go up. As of the end of the second quarter, the company held $12.2 billion in "funds receivable and amounts held on behalf of customers," on which it earns interest. That's a substantial advantage of its business model and gives it resilience when many of its tech stock peers are falling in the face of higher interest rates.

2. It won't be disrupted by agentic AI

The launch of Meta Platforms' Muse also exposed a hidden advantage of Airbnb. Unlike its online travel agency (OTA) rivals Expedia and Booking, Airbnb's inventory is mostly specific to its platform. Expedia and Booking, on the other hand, are essentially middlemen, connecting users to hotels and acting as a clearinghouse for hotels that want to get their listings in front of prospective customers.

2 Internet Stocks Worth Your Attention and 1 Facing Headwinds

Whether it be online shopping or social media, secular forces are propelling consumer internet businesses forward. This influence cuts both ways though because they have high exposure to the ups and downs of consumer spending, and the market seems to believe the tide is turning in the wrong direction - over the past six months, the industry has tumbled by 2.2%. This drop is a noticeable divergence from the S&P 500's 8.9% return.

Only some companies are subject to these dynamics, however, and a handful of high-quality businesses can deliver earnings growth in any environment. Taking that into account, here are two internet stocks we think can generate sustainable market-beating returns and one we would avoid.

One Consumer Internet Stock to Sell:
Chewy (CHWY)

Market Cap: $8.43 billion

Founded by Ryan Cohen, who later became known for his involvement in GameStop, Chewy (NYSE:CHWY) is an online retailer specializing in pet food, supplies, and healthcare services.

Why Are We Hesitant About CHWY?

Annual sales growth of 6.5% over the last three years lagged behind its consumer internet peers as its large revenue base made it difficult to generate incremental demand

Projected sales growth of 7% for the next 12 months suggests sluggish demand

Gross margin of 29.7% is below its competitors, leaving less money to invest in areas like marketing and R&D

Two Consumer Internet Stocks to Watch:
Booking (BKNG)

Market Cap: $122.8 billion

Why Do We Like BKNG?

Superior platform functionality and low servicing costs lead to a best-in-class gross margin of 87%

Disciplined cost controls and effective management resulted in a strong two-year EBITDA margin of 36.4%, and its operating leverage amplified its profits over the last few years

Robust free cash flow margin of 35.3% gives it many options for capital deployment

At $163.47 per share, Booking trades at 11.6x forward EV/EBITDA. Is now a good time to buy? Find out in our full research report, it's free.

Airbnb (ABNB)

Market Cap: $102.4 billion

Founded by Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia in their San Francisco apartment, Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) is the world's largest online marketplace for lodging, primarily homestays.

Why Will ABNB Outperform?

Nights and Experiences Booked have grown by 9.3% annually, allowing for more profitable cross-selling opportunities if it can build complementary products and features

Healthy EBITDA margin of 35.6% shows it's a well-run company with efficient processes, and its rise over the last few years was fueled by some leverage on its fixed costs

ABNB is a free cash flow machine with the flexibility to invest in growth initiatives or return capital to shareholders

Airbnb (ABNB) put its fall product update front and center this week, spotlighting AI-powered search and new on-trip services that tighten the link between its travel platform and day-to-day trip logistics.

Recent price action has been broadly supportive of that story, with a 30.59% year to date share price return and a 37.96% total shareholder return over the past year, suggesting that momentum has been building as Airbnb rolls out product upgrades and investors reassess its risk and growth profile.

See how Airbnb's AI-driven travel push fits alongside other fast-moving consumer services by reviewing our hand-picked list of 20 high quality undiscovered gems with strong fundamentals and room for a rerating.

Airbnb now trades close to analyst targets, yet internal fair value estimates still suggest a sizable gap. Is this latest AI-fueled rally already pricing in the story, or is that 40% implied discount too wide?

Most Popular Narrative: 4.5% Undervalued

Airbnb's most followed valuation storyline pegs fair value at $181.84 per share compared with the recent $173.70 close. This points to a modest upside gap that still needs to be justified by the underlying business mix and product momentum.

"This is the first time in a while where Airbnb is not asking investors to believe that the next growth engine is coming. Some of it is actually showing up. Core markets are accelerating again. International markets are still growing quickly. AI is reducing costs. The core product is converting better. Hotels are gaining traction. Experiences are at least moving in the right direction. And profitability remains very strong."

See why 86 investors see Airbnb as 4% undervalued.

According to TickerTickle, that fair value view rests on a few key levers. The narrative uses a 12% annual revenue growth rate, a 24.5% long term net margin and a future P/E of 27x, all discounted at 8.5%. Those inputs combine into a fair value estimate of $181.84, only slightly above the current share price yet still meaningfully below the $290.97 future cash flow value implied by the SWS DCF model.

This creates an interesting split for readers. The DCF output and Simply Wall St valuation checks flag Airbnb as trading 40.3% below future cash flow value. The popular narrative frames the gap as a 4.5% discount to fair value. That tension often reflects different expectations for how quickly earnings and free cash flow convert into shareholder returns, rather than a disagreement about the direction of the business itself.

Airbnb recently rolled out a fall product update that connects travelers with friends' trips, introduces AI-powered search, and adds on-trip services like Instacart grocery delivery, laundry, baby gear rentals, and local experiences.

The tighter integration of AI search with services such as grocery and gear delivery points to Airbnb pushing deeper into higher-fee, non-lodging spend across each trip.

We will now look at how Airbnb's investment narrative is shaped by these AI-powered search upgrades and expanded on-trip services.

Scan beyond Airbnb's AI-fueled travel update and see how other platforms are using data and automation to reshape bookings, logistics, and spend patterns with a curated list of 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

Airbnb Investment Narrative Recap

To own Airbnb, you have to believe it can keep turning a global host network, strong direct traffic, and an expanding services layer into consistent earnings while staying ahead of new AI booking agents and regulation. The fall product update sits right on that thesis. It tightens the link between discovery, booking, and on-trip spend, but does not change the core near term driver, which is execution on the broader travel platform vision.

The biggest short term swing factor is how effectively Airbnb can grow higher fee experiences, hotels, and services without eroding guest or host satisfaction. The main risk remains external pressure, from AI intermediaries that could sit between Airbnb and users, and from city level rules that may limit supply. The new features are helpful but not decisive against either issue yet.

The most relevant piece of the recent rollout is the AI powered search that lets you describe a trip in natural language and see homes, experiences, and services in one view. For investors, this speaks directly to two things that matter for Airbnb: how efficiently the marketplace matches supply and demand, and how much of a trip's wallet the platform can realistically capture.

Execution is what counts. If AI summaries and side by side comparisons reduce search friction, guests may be more willing to book longer stays, try hotels on Airbnb, or attach services like grocery delivery and laundry. That supports the existing catalyst around experiences and services raising revenue per booking, but it also raises the bar on product quality. Any mismatch between AI recommendations, actual listings, and on trip services would quickly show up in reviews and support costs.

Airbnb's narrative projects US$18.6b revenue and US$4.7b earnings by 2029. That path assumes revenue growing at 12.3% per year and an earnings increase of about US$2b from US$2.7b today.
